application_questions.question: Seven properties sold in a Ballarat suburb in one week for (in thousands of dollars): $510, 530, 540, 540, 560, 580, 1400$ (where $\$1\,400\,000$ was a heritage acreage estate). Find (a) the median and mean of all $7$ prices, and (b) the new median and new mean when the $\$1\,400\,000$ outlier is removed.
application_questions.answer: (a) Median $= \$540\text{k}$, Mean $= \$665.71\text{k}$; (b) New Median $= \$540\text{k}$ (unchanged!), New Mean $= \$543.33\text{k}$

application_questions.question: Over his first $5$ netball matches, Noah's team scored $42, 38, 45, 51$, and $39$ goals. How many goals must the team score in the $6$th match to achieve a mean of $44$ goals per match across all $6$ matches?

In a Year 8 science cohort, Class 8A ($20$ students) has a mean test score of $76$, and Class 8B ($30$ students) has a mean test score of $81$. Calculate the combined mean score for all $50$ students.

A stem-and-leaf plot of daily commuter cycling times (in minutes, where $2 \mid 5 = 25$) for $9$ trips is: $1 \mid 8, 9$; $2 \mid 1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 8$; $6 \mid 5$. Find the median, mean, and range of the $9$ trips, and identify the outlier.
application_questions.answer: Outlier $= 65\text{ min}$; Median $= 24\text{ min}$, Mean $= 26.56\text{ min}$ ($\frac{239}{9}$), Range $= 47\text{ min}$

application_questions.question: A local council in Geelong wants to know whether residents support building a new skate park. Survey Method 1 posts an online poll on a skateboarding club page; Survey Method 2 mails a survey to $400$ households chosen by random lot-number generator across all suburbs. Identify the sampling bias in Method 1 and state why Method 2 is more representative.
application_questions.answer: Method 1 suffers from self-selection and undercoverage bias (only skateboard enthusiasts respond, overestimating support). Method 2 uses random sampling across all suburbs, giving every household an equal chance.

application_questions.question: A regional sports club has $450$ members: $180$ Juniors, $150$ Seniors, and $120$ Masters. The committee selects a stratified random sample of $60$ members to survey about training times. How many Juniors, Seniors, and Masters should be included in the sample?

Daily January maximum temperatures ($^\circ\text{C}$) over $7$ days in Mildura ($32, 35, 36, 38, 39, 41, 45$) and Hobart ($19, 21, 22, 22, 24, 25, 28$) are recorded. Calculate the median and range for both cities and write a two-sentence comparison of their centre and spread.
application_questions.answer: Mildura: Median $= 38^\circ\text{C}$, Range $= 13^\circ\text{C}$. Hobart: Median $= 22^\circ\text{C}$, Range $= 9^\circ\text{C}$. Mildura is substantially hotter on average ($16^\circ\text{C}$ higher median) and also has slightly greater temperature variability ($13^\circ\text{C}$ vs $9^\circ\text{C}$ range).

application_questions.question: A histogram of $200$ suburban house prices in Melbourne is strongly positively skewed with a median of $\$920\,000$ and a mean of $\$1\,180\,000$. Explain why news reports quote the median house price rather than the mean, and state what causes the positive skew.
application_questions.answer: A small number of multi-million-dollar luxury properties create a long upper tail (positive skew) that inflates the mean to $\$1\,180\,000$, whereas the median ($\$920\,000$) accurately reflects the middle property.

reasoning_questions.question: To select a systematic sample of $40$ items from a factory production run of $1200$ items, an inspector calculates the step size $k = \dfrac{1200}{40} = 30$, picks a random starting number $r$ between $1$ and $30$ (say $r = 12$), and selects items $12, 42, 72, \dots$. Explain why the starting number $r$ MUST be chosen at random rather than always starting at item $1$, and what could go wrong if the factory machinery has a periodic cycle every $30$ items.
reasoning_questions.answer: A random start ensures every item has an equal $\frac{1}{30}$ chance of selection. If the machine has a defect cycle every $30$ items, sampling every $30$th item could hit the exact same point in the cycle every time (either all defective or none defective), biasing the sample.

reasoning_questions.question: Two classes sit the same $100$-mark maths exam. Both classes have a mean of $70$ and a median of $70$, but Class X has a range of $18$ while Class Y has a range of $64$. Sketch or describe how their dot plots differ, and explain why quoting only a measure of centre (mean or median) is insufficient when comparing two datasets.
reasoning_questions.answer: Class X's scores are tightly clustered around $70$ (e.g. $61$ to $79$), whereas Class Y's scores are widely spread from very low to very high (e.g. $36$ to $100$). Without a measure of spread (range), two very different distributions look identical from their centre alone.
